text:
ashley: quick retrospective from the canary last night — we saw the fair scheduler preferring small tenants too aggressively and a few mid-size customers hit elevated tail latency.
kevin: saw that in traces. at ~23:12 we had a drift where weight updates weren't applied to the local admission window for ~2m.
priya: yup, reproducer in staging: when policy-rollout=fast the local cache update path drops the admission-change event.
ben: is the problem the event queue or the interface between policy-service and local-admit?
rachel: looked at logs — policy-service emitted correct delta, but the agent's apply_lock took a timeout and retried. race on backoff caused window to shrink.
ashley: (minor correction) i'm ashley, not "nashley" :slightly_smiling_face:
kevin: heh. main question: do we fix by making the local agent more robust, or by tightening the contract so policy changes are idempotent and replayable?
priya: preference for stronger contract. If we make policy messages replayable and include versioned diffs then transient failures won't cause divergence.
ben: agree on versioning. tradeoff is complexity in the admission protocol and storage costs for diffs.
rachel: alternative: extend lease TTLs during rollouts so transient gaps don't impact runtime weights. cheaper, but hides root cause.
ashley: ops-bot: deploy canary summary: canary v2.4.1 -> 23:00-00:30; 3/120 requests > SLA (baseline 1/100), affected: tenant-omega, tenant-koi.
ops-bot: added trace links: https://redwood/traces/abcd1234 and logs: https://redwood/logs/efgh5678
kevin: i'm worried about abuse surface too. currently abuse-detector runs downstream of admission and is best-effort. if we delay policy updates we could misclassify temporary bursts.
priya: thought: split responsibilities — admission API: token_vector + priority_hint; fairness scheduler: consumes authoritative token_vector and exposes read-only snapshot API; abuse detector: subscribes to raw ingress telemetry (pre-admission) and pushes signals to policy-service.
ben: that separation seems cleaner. concrete interfaces:
```
// admission request
{ tenant_id, tokens_consumed, priority_hint }
// fairness snapshot
{ version, weights: [{tenant, weight}], effective_ts }
// abuse signal
{ tenant_id, spike_score, window_start }
```
kevin: two concerns: 1) snapshot staleness (clients reading old snapshot), 2) complexity of wiring abuse signals into policy eval loop.
rachel: snapshot staleness mitigated by including version and fallbacks. if snapshot.version < expected then agent can apply conservative admission (reduce allowed batch size) and request immediate refresh.
ashley: for the abuse signals, policy-service should not be the only consumer. we should allow local agent plug-ins to subscribe and take emergency action (soft-shed) to avoid operator round-trips.
priya: agreed, but must constrain what local agents can do. propose a capability set: [soft_shed, throttle_hint, priority_override] that is auditable.
ben: logging/audit is key. make sure any local emergency action emits a signed event back to policy-service so rollbacks are traceable.
kevin: operational metrics wishlist: per-tenant snapshot lag, count of emergency local actions, rejected-replay events, policy-diff queue depth.
rachel: i'll add those to the telemetry RFC. also add a test plan: chaotic rollouts where policy-service drops 1 in N messages to agents and we validate convergence within T.
ashley: timeline: 1) short-term patch: increase apply_lock backoff and emit more debug when apply fails (1 week). 2) medium: snapshot versioning + conservative fallback behavior (3 weeks). 3) long-term: refactor into separated admission/fairness/abuse interfaces + emergency capabilities (+ telemetry) (Q2).
ben: for the long-term refactor we should define a proto contract. i'll draft an interface PR with Go/gRPC protos and a JSON-over-HTTP shim for hosted.
priya: also consider model for backwards compatibility: policy-service should be able to serve both v1 (push diffs) and v2 (snapshots). agents should negotiate via handshake.
kevin: thumbs up. one more: we should document abuse signal semantics carefully — what constitutes spike_score, sampling windows, and how to avoid punishing ramping traffic.
rachel: i'll volunteer to own the abuse semantics doc.
ashley: thanks team. action items: ben proto PR, rachel telemetry + abuse semantics, priya snapshot logic, kevin lock/backoff patch. i'll follow up with weekly check-in. :thumbsup:
kevin: +1
priya: thanks all
ben: will start PR today
rachel: added to my board
ops-bot: reminder: weekly eng-platform sync Friday 14:00 GMT
kevin: closing the thread here, re-open if anything else crops up.
